# On the Joy of Getting Lost

I've been thinking about how we're losing the art of being lost.

GPS has made it nearly impossible to wander without a destination. We optimize our routes, shave minutes off commutes, arrive exactly when predicted. It's efficient. It's also sterile.

There's something valuable in taking a wrong turn and discovering a bakery you'll visit for years, or a park bench that becomes your thinking spot. Some of my best memories involve being genuinely uncertain about where I was—not in a panic way, but in that suspended moment where anything felt possible.

Children seem to understand this instinctively. They'll follow a butterfly for ten minutes and somehow end up somewhere fascinating, or at least somewhere different from where they started. Adults have trained this out of themselves, always rushing toward predetermined coordinates.

I'm not advocating for inefficiency—I love a good GPS when I'm trying to reach an airport on time. But I wonder if we've overcorrected. If we've sacrificed serendipity for punctuality.

The best conversations I've had started with "I don't really know this area" and ended somewhere unexpected. The best writing often happens when you're not sure where you're going. The best relationships sometimes begin by chance, at a place you'd never planned to be.

Maybe the antidote to modern life isn't more optimization. Maybe it's occasionally turning off the map, taking the unmarked path, and seeing what happens when you don't know exactly where you'll end up.
